conditions.label: Acute iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis of left lower extremity

medications.drug_text: 0.6 ML fondaparinux sodium 12.5 MG/ML Prefilled Syringe
medications.sig: Inject 7.5 mg under the skin once daily

reports.text: Left lower extremity venous duplex. The left common femoral vein and proximal femoral vein are non-compressible and distended with echogenic intraluminal thrombus and absent color flow. Popliteal vein and calf veins compress normally. Contralateral common femoral vein compressible with normal phasic flow.
reports.conclusion: Acute deep vein thrombosis of the left common femoral and proximal femoral veins.

documents.title: Emergency Department Note and Observation Discharge
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital ED / observation unit
Arrived 4/4/2024 09:40, discharged 4/5/2024 13:15

68F, CKD 3b, DM2, class II obesity, longstanding bilateral ankle swelling from tricuspid regurgitation. Woke today with the left calf suddenly swollen and throbbing, tight, worse to walk on. Landed two days ago from a 12-hour flight home from abroad. No injury. Denies chest pain, breathlessness, coughing blood.

Vitals stable as charted.
Exam: left leg visibly bigger than right, pitting to the knee, calf tender, Homans positive. Rest of exam unremarkable apart from her known murmur.

Labs: PT/INR, aPTT, platelets normal. Creatinine at her stage 3b baseline.
Duplex: acute thrombus L common femoral and proximal femoral veins.

Assessment: acute left iliofemoral DVT, provoked by long-haul travel. No features of PE.

Plan: fondaparinux 7.5 mg SC daily (weight 98 kg; dose acceptable at her CrCl, with monitoring). Kept overnight in observation to teach injections and watch for bleeding - none; pain already easing. Thigh-high compression stockings. Expected treatment course 3 months, PCP to manage. Return for chest pain, shortness of breath, bleeding.

NKDA.

documents.title: PA - fondaparinux
documents.author: MA
documents.body: Pharmacy says Part D plan needs PA for fondaparinux 7.5 mg syringes. Submitted with ED duplex and dx (acute L iliofemoral DVT), 90 days requested. Approved 4/5 at 16:40 through 7/10/24. Pt has 3 syringes from the hospital, picking up the rest tonight.

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
ED/obs records reviewed: L common femoral and proximal femoral DVT after the long flight home, started fondaparinux 7.5 daily.

Doing the injections herself into the belly, small bruises, no other bleeding. Leg still swollen but less tender, wearing the stocking. No chest pain or breathlessness beyond her usual stairs.

Exam: SpO2 normal. L leg larger than R, pitting to knee, mild calf tenderness. Lungs clear. Murmur as before.

A/P: provoked L iliofemoral DVT. 3 months of fondaparinux, then stop. Watch for bleeding, keep acetaminophen only for pain (no NSAIDs, no aspirin). Walk as tolerated. Recheck in early July.

documents.title: bruises
documents.author: patient
documents.body: My belly has bruises where I do the shots, some as big as a quarter. Is that normal? No other bleeding.

documents.title: RE: bruises
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Small bruises at the injection spots are common with this medicine. Rotate sides, stay 2 inches from the belly button, don't rub after the shot. Call us right away for bleeding from gums or nose that won't stop, blood in urine or stool, black stools, or a bruise that keeps growing.

reports.text: Compared with 4/2022. LV normal size, LVEF 55-60%. RV dilated, mildly reduced function, unchanged. RA dilated. Severe tricuspid regurgitation, unchanged. RVSP estimated 38 mmHg. No pericardial effusion.

Echo: TR and right heart unchanged since 2022.

No changes from a valve standpoint. Next echo 2 years, clinic yearly. NKDA.

Cardiology

events.reason: Sudden chest pain and shortness of breath

medications.drug: pantoprazole 40 MG Delayed Release Oral Tablet
medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth daily before breakfast

reports.text: Portable AP chest. Air-fluid level projecting behind the cardiac silhouette. Reduced aeration at the left base. No pneumothorax.
reports.conclusion: Retrocardiac air-fluid level, suggesting an intrathoracic stomach/hiatal hernia. CT recommended.

reports.text: Sinus rhythm, rate 98. Right bundle branch block, unchanged from 2021. No acute ST elevation or depression.
reports.conclusion: Sinus rhythm, RBBB, no acute ischemic change.

reports.text: CT angiogram of the chest with IV contrast. No filling defect in the pulmonary arteries. Large paraesophageal hiatal hernia with most of the stomach above the diaphragm, compressing the adjacent left lower lobe. The stomach enhances normally; no organoaxial or mesenteroaxial twist, no wall thickening, pneumatosis or free air. Right heart chambers dilated. No pleural effusion.
reports.conclusion: No pulmonary embolism. Large paraesophageal hiatal hernia with intrathoracic stomach, no volvulus or ischemia.

documents.title: Emergency Department Provider Note
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital ED

69F, reflux, prior L leg DVT (2024), severe TR, CKD 3b, DM2. Four hours of abrupt, severe, sharp chest pain with shortness of breath; worse lying back, better leaning forward/sitting up. On questioning, about a year of food sticking now and then and feeling full quickly after meals, which she chalked up to reflux.

BP 150/90, HR 98, RR 22, SpO2 94% RA.
Abdomen soft, nontender. Breath sounds reduced at the L base. Known LLSB murmur.

Labs: Hgb 13.2, WBC 9.0, plt 250, glucose 180, Cr 1.52, ALT 30, AST 28. hs-troponin normal x2. ECG: RBBB, old.
CXR: retrocardiac air-fluid level.
CTA chest: no PE. Large paraesophageal hernia, most of the stomach in the chest, no volvulus or ischemia.

Assessment: symptomatic large paraesophageal hiatal hernia. PE excluded. Surgery consulted, admitting.
Started pantoprazole 40 daily. NKDA.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
Regional hospital, General Surgery
Admitted 4/3/2025 via ED, discharged 4/6/2025

Diagnosis: large paraesophageal hiatal hernia, symptomatic, without volvulus or strangulation.

Course: kept NPO initially with IV fluids; insulin glargine reduced while not eating, metformin held. Pain settled within 24 hours. Diet advanced to soft solids, tolerated. Breathing comfortable, SpO2 mid-90s on room air. Creatinine stable.

Given her symptoms and the size of the hernia, we recommend elective laparoscopic repair with fundoplication. She agrees; surgery scheduled for 5/19/2025.

Discharge medications: home medications at prior doses (lisinopril 20, amlodipine 5, furosemide 40, metformin 1000 BID, glargine 18 u, atorvastatin 40, cholecalciferol, acetaminophen prn), plus NEW pantoprazole 40 mg daily.
Diet: small soft meals, upright 2 hours after eating.
Return for recurrent severe chest pain, vomiting, inability to swallow.
NKDA.
General Surgery

documents.title: Post-Hospital Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen after 4/3-4/6 admission: large paraesophageal hernia found on CXR/CT, PE ruled out. ED and surgery summaries reviewed.

No chest pain since discharge. Eating small soft meals, no sticking. Taking pantoprazole. Sugars a little high the first days home, settling.

Exam: BP and SpO2 as charted. Breath sounds slightly reduced L base. Abdomen soft. Murmur as before.

A/P
1. Paraesophageal hiatal hernia - elective lap repair 5/19. Continue pantoprazole, small meals, upright after eating. ED if severe chest pain or can't keep food down.
2. DM2: back on usual regimen. Around surgery follow the surgeon's insulin instructions.
3. Med rec done with her bottles.

documents.title: surgery on the 19th
documents.author: patient
documents.body: The surgeon's office gave me a sheet that says take half my long insulin the night before surgery and no metformin that morning. Is that ok with you?

documents.title: RE: surgery on the 19th
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Yes, that plan is fine. Half the glargine (9 units) the night before, skip metformin the morning of surgery, and check your sugar when you wake up. Good luck, we'll call you the week after.

documents.title: Operative and Discharge Summary
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
Regional hospital, General Surgery
Admitted 5/19/2025, discharged 5/21/2025

Procedure 5/19: laparoscopic paraesophageal hernia repair with reduction of the stomach and sac, crural closure and fundoplication. Prior upper abdominal (open cholecystectomy) adhesions taken down. No complications. Port sites closed.

Course: clear liquids POD0, full liquids POD1. Pain controlled with acetaminophen. Glucose managed with reduced glargine while on liquids. Ambulating. Sequential compression devices in house given her DVT history.

Discharge: post-fundoplication diet (liquids 1 week, then soft for 3 weeks). Continue pantoprazole 40 mg daily until clinic. Resume home medications; glargine 18 units once eating soft foods.
Clinic in 4-5 weeks.
NKDA.
General Surgery

documents.title: RN Check-in

documents.body: Called pt 1 week after hernia surgery. Port sites clean, small amount of bruising. On full liquids, moving to soft food Wednesday per surgeon. Fasting sugars 100-130, back on full glargine since yesterday per discharge instructions, no lows. No calf pain or swelling, walking hallway several times daily. Reminded to call with fever, vomiting, inability to swallow.

Regional hospital ED / observation
Arrived 3/27/2026 10:15, discharged 3/28/2026 12:40

70F with DM2, CKD 3b, class II obesity and a prior L iliofemoral DVT (2024), now with the left calf again: abrupt swelling and throbbing since this morning, tight, hurts to walk. Got back two days ago from another 12-hour international flight. No injury. No chest pain, no dyspnea, no hemoptysis.

Vitals stable as charted.
Exam: L leg swollen with pitting to the knee, calf tender, Homans positive. Otherwise unremarkable apart from her known murmur.

Coags normal at baseline, platelets normal, creatinine at her baseline.
Duplex: acute thrombus L proximal femoral vein.

Assessment: recurrent left lower extremity DVT after long-haul travel.

Plan: fondaparinux 7.5 mg SC daily restarted (she used it in 2024). Observed overnight, no bleeding, pain improving. Compression stockings. Second VTE - duration of anticoagulation to be decided with her PCP. Return precautions for chest pain, SOB, bleeding. NKDA.

Leg less tight, still swollen. Injecting fine, minor bruising. No chest pain, breathing her usual.

Exam: SpO2 normal. L calf larger and mildly tender. Lungs clear.

Because this is the second one, I'm leaning toward long-term anticoagulation rather than stopping at 3 months; she'd prefer a pill over shots. We'll decide at the 3-4 month mark. No NSAIDs/aspirin. Bleeding precautions reviewed.
RTC ~4 months, sooner prn.

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
4 months out from the second L leg DVT. Swelling down to her usual, no pain. Tired of daily shots. No bleeding other than injection bruises.

Exam: BP and weight as charted. Calves soft, symmetric, trace ankle edema as always. Murmur unchanged. Lungs clear.

A/P
1. Recurrent DVT (2024, 2026), both travel-related. Two events - recommend indefinite anticoagulation; she agrees. Switch fondaparinux to apixaban 5 mg BID: take the first tablet tomorrow at the time her next injection would be due, then no more injections. Apixaban fine at her kidney function. Discussed bleeding signs, no NSAIDs/aspirin, tell dentists. Will reassess dose and need yearly.
2. DM2: A1c today, same regimen.
3. CKD 3b: BMP, CBC today (also baseline on apixaban).
4. HTN at goal. TR stable per June echo.

RTC October.
